context.description:
Jackstones, Inc. (JAS), formerly NextStage, Inc. (NXT), was originally incorporated on April 22, 1964 as Pacific Cement Company, Inc. to engage in the manufacture and trading of cement and related products. In June 2000, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the change in primary purpose of the Company to that of a holding company and changed its corporate name to PACEMCO Holdings, Inc. (PACEMCO). In December 2000, PACEMCO acquired 100% of the capital stock of NXT, and in 2001, the SEC approved the merger of PACEMCO and NXT, with the former as the surviving corporation. Subsequently, the SEC approved the change in name from PACEMCO to NXT.

On April 16, 2014, the SEC approved the Company's change in corporate name to its present name. The Company also moved to change the stock symbol to its current one effective May 13, 2014.

JAS has one wholly-owned subsidiary, Jackstones Properties, Inc., a property developer which owns Michelia Residences located in Marikina City.

Source: SEC Form 17-A (2024)

## Company: Jackstones, Inc. (JAS)
Sector: Property / Property
Jackstones, Inc. (JAS), formerly NextStage, Inc. (NXT), was originally incorporated on April 22, 1964 as Pacific Cement Company, Inc. to engage in the manufacture and trading of cement and related products. In June 2000, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) approved the change in primary purpose of the Company to that of a holding company and changed its corporate name to PACEMCO Holdings, Inc. (PACEMCO). In December 2000, PACEMCO acquired 100% of the capital stock of NXT, and in 2001, the SEC approved the merger of PACEMCO and NXT, with the former as the surviving corporation. Subsequently, the SEC approved the change in name from PACEMCO to NXT.

On April 16, 2014, the SEC approved the Company's change in corporate name to its present name. The Company also moved to change the stock symbol to its current one effective May 13, 2014.

JAS has one wholly-owned subsidiary, Jackstones Properties, Inc., a property developer which owns Michelia Residences located in Marikina City.

storedThesis:
Jackstones, Inc. is extraordinarily difficult to understand as a business, and that opacity is itself a red flag. The company has cycled through four corporate identities — Pacific Cement, PACEMCO Holdings, NextStage, and now Jackstones — without ever developing a clear, durable operating business. Today it is effectively a listed shell with one operating subsidiary, Jackstones Properties, Inc., which owns a single townhouse project in Marikina City. A company whose entire productive asset is one mid-market residential development in a single Metro Manila city is not a business with breadth or compounding power — it is a real estate project wearing a stock listing as a costume.

The moat question answers itself. JAS has no brand, no network effect, no switching costs, no proprietary process, and no cost advantage. Michelia Residences is a generic mid-market townhouse development in a market served by dozens of better-capitalized developers (Ayala Land, SMDC, DMCI, Rockwell). Worse, the -21.2% average ROIC over the past decade means the company has been destroying capital at an alarming rate — a structurally un-moated business that earns negative returns on the capital entrusted to it cannot compound value for shareholders regardless of price.

Management quality is poor. PSE sanctioned JAS in 2022 for violating basic disclosure rules — specifically failing to give adequate notice of stockholder meetings and late submission of stockholder lists. The five most recent disclosures on record are all filed generically as "Material Information/Transactions," which tells the market almost nothing. This pattern of minimal disclosure is characteristic of a company that treats its public listing as a convenience, not a responsibility. The controlling shareholder group, led by Mariano Tanenglian (who had a public falling out with his brother Lucio Tan before acquiring control in 2014), has given no public evidence of a long-term value-creation plan. The recurring "material transactions" filings without substantive follow-through suggest the company may be positioning for another backdoor asset injection — which benefits insiders, not minority shareholders.

The valuation is indefensible by any Rule #1 metric. JAS reports no earnings, making P/E and a Rule #1 Sticker Price incalculable. What is calculable is damning: P/B of 14.3x for a business generating deeply negative returns on invested capital. You are being asked to pay ₱14.30 for every peso of book value in a company that consistently destroys that book value. No margin of safety exists because intrinsic value cannot be estimated positively — a business with chronic negative ROIC and no earnings path has an intrinsic value near zero on a going-concern basis. The only thesis for buying JAS is a speculative bet on a backdoor listing of new assets, which is not investing — it is gambling on insider intentions.

Pass without hesitation. JAS fails all four Ms simultaneously: the business is opaque and has no stable identity, the moat is nonexistent, management has demonstrated poor governance, and the price reflects zero margin of safety on a capital-destroying entity. The only scenario where JAS becomes interesting is if credible, clean assets are reverse-merged at a disclosed fair value — and even then, you would be entering at the insiders' terms. Watch from a distance only if a transformative, fully-disclosed asset injection is announced with clear financials.
